description: Learning Waypoints width tiers — Mathematics Year 2
subject: Mathematics

width_notes.minimum_width: Narrowest honest floor for the command term at Year 2. Set by what MUST be demonstrated — not what is easiest or most common. For concept/understanding descriptors: the minimum range of phenomena or examples that meets the command term. For modelling and process descriptors: the minimum task context that constitutes genuine engagement with the descriptor.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope as ACARA intended for Year 2 Mathematics. Grounded in the most common elaboration cases. Reflects sound standard practice — what a class that has engaged with the descriptor fully would have done.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena, contexts or cultural perspectives — not difficulty. Each wider item is a discrete direction. First Nations knowledge and cultural contexts appear as wider directions where ACARA elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA v9 elaborations used as primary source data for all three tiers. Verbatim elaborations preserved per entry for traceability.

AC9M2N01.minimum_width: Recognise, represent and order three-digit numbers using one physical or virtual material; read and write the numeral; locate on a 0–1000 number line.
AC9M2N01.typical_width: Recognise, represent and order numbers to at least 1000 across physical materials, numerals, number lines and hundreds charts; includes numbers with zeros in different positions; read, write and order two-, three- and four-digit numbers using patterns in the number system.
wider: Order numbers that look or sound similar (e.g. 808, 880, 818, 881); explain the strategy used to distinguish them by place value
Collect and group large quantities of recyclable objects into ones, tens and hundreds; show different representations of the resulting three-digit number
Use hundreds chart puzzle pieces to locate number positions; describe location using place-value reasoning
elaborations: recognising missing numbers on different number lines; e.g. a number line with 1800 on one end and 220 on the other, with every decade numbered
recognising and locating the position of pieces within hundreds chart puzzles using knowledge of the order of natural numbers

reading and writing numerals, and saying and ordering two-, three- and four-digit numbers using patterns in the number system, including numbers with zeros in different places, and numbers that look and sound similar such as 808, 880, 818 and 881
collecting large quantities of materials for recycling and grouping them into ones, tens and hundreds; using the materials to show different representations of two- and three-digit numbers

AC9M2N02.minimum_width: Partition one three-digit number into hundreds, tens and ones; write in expanded form; identify the role of a zero digit in one example.
AC9M2N02.typical_width: Partition, rearrange, regroup and rename two- and three-digit numbers using standard and non-standard groupings; explain the meaning of each digit; rename numbers in multiple ways (e.g. 245 as 24 tens and 5 ones); explain why zero holds a position even when no quantity occupies it.
wider: Find all possible renamings of a given three-digit number using different groupings; record systematically and identify patterns
Compare the digits of a number with base-ten materials in all three grouping styles; explain equivalence for each
elaborations: comparing the digits of a number with materials grouped into hundreds, tens and ones, and explaining the meaning of each of the digits in the materials
renaming numbers in different ways using knowledge of place value; for example, renaming 245 as 24 tens and 5 ones or 2 hundreds and 45 ones

AC9M2N03.minimum_width: Identify one-half of a shape or collection by dividing into 2 equal parts; fold or share to create quarters; name each part.
AC9M2N03.typical_width: Recognise one-half as one of 2 equal parts; create halves, quarters and eighths through repeated halving of shapes, objects and collections; name parts; demonstrate that a quarter is a half of a half and an eighth is a half of a quarter; relate number of equal parts to the unit fraction.
wider: Compare half of a set of 12 with half of a set of 8; discuss why both are one-half even though the amounts differ in absolute terms
Use repeated halving to subdivide shapes in different ways; discuss the inverse relationship between number of parts and part size
Divide shapes into 4 equal parts and 8 equal parts; compare one-quarter with one-eighth; connect to the unit fraction rule
elaborations: creating halves of a range of collections by sharing into 2 equal groups; comparing half of a set of 12 washers with half of a set of 8 bolts
creating halves using measurement attributes; explaining that a half is one part out of 2 equal parts of a whole
using repeated halving to subdivide shapes and objects into halves, quarters and eighths; naming parts and comparing sizes
dividing a shape into equal parts and relating the number of parts to the unit fraction

AC9M2N04.minimum_width: Add or subtract a one-digit number from a two-digit number using one mental strategy; represent as a number sentence.
AC9M2N04.typical_width: Add and subtract one- and two-digit numbers using a range of strategies (near doubles, bridging tens, partitioning, number lines); represent problems as number sentences and bar models; explain the connection between the sentence and the situation; use informal jottings to track steps.
wider: Apply the associative property to rearrange addends for easier mental calculation (e.g. 7+8 = 7+(7+1) = (7+7)+1)
Solve multi-step money problems using a number line; explain each step
Explore First Nations Australians' stories and dances representing the balance between addition and subtraction; represent as number sentences
elaborations: using the associative property of addition to assist with mental calculation by partitioning, rearranging and regrouping
using strategies such as doubles, near doubles, part-part-whole to 10, bridging tens and partitioning for two-digit numbers
representing addition and subtraction problems using a bar model and writing a number sentence
using mental strategies and informal jottings for two-digit problems; recognising zero added leaves a number unchanged
using a number line or hundreds chart to solve addition or subtraction problems
using First Nations Australians' stories and dances to understand the balance between addition and subtraction

AC9M2N05.minimum_width: Make equal groups for a multiplication problem; write a repeated addition sentence; solve one sharing division problem using materials.
AC9M2N05.typical_width: Multiply and divide using repeated addition, equal grouping, arrays and partitioning; make and name arrays; use bar models; distinguish partitive from quotitive division; use skip counting and materials to calculate.
wider: Make all different arrays for the same total (e.g. 12); name each and connect to multiplication facts
Partition a larger array using subitising and known facts to find the total
Compare partitive and quotitive division for the same numbers; discuss what the answer means in each case
elaborations: making and naming arrays and using bar models to solve simple multiplication or sharing problems
finding the total in an array by partitioning using subitising and number facts
recognising the difference between dividing into 3 equal groups and dividing into groups of 3
using a Think Board to solve partition and quotition division problems
using materials or diagrams and skip counting to solve repeated equal quantity multiplication problems

AC9M2N06.minimum_width: Identify the operation for a practical problem; represent with a number sentence; calculate and state the answer in terms of the situation.
AC9M2N06.typical_width: Model practical additive and multiplicative problems including money transactions; represent situations with diagrams and number sentences; choose and apply calculation strategies; interpret and communicate solutions including handling remainders.
wider: Model money problems with whole dollar amounts: purchases, class contributions, budgeting
Model equal grouping/sharing in practical contexts (teams, food); decide what to do with remainders and justify
Model 'How many days left in this year?' using a calendar and addition
Model grouping problems from First Nations Australian children's instructive games (e.g. Yangamini, Tiwi Island Peoples); represent as a number sentence and interpret the solution
elaborations: modelling an everyday additive or multiplicative situation; deciding the operation and justifying the choice
modelling simple money problems with whole dollar amounts
modelling practical problems: team sizes, sharing food or money; deciding what to do with remainders
modelling 'How many days are left in this year?' using a calendar
modelling problems from First Nations Australian children's instructive games; e.g. Yangamini

AC9M2A01.minimum_width: Identify the constant term in a given additive number sequence (increasing or decreasing) and state the rule.
AC9M2A01.typical_width: Recognise, describe and create additive patterns in number sequences, shape sequences and object arrangements; identify the constant term; use it to find missing elements; recognise both increasing and decreasing patterns.
wider: Recognise additive patterns in the built environment (windows per carriage, wheels per car); record in tables; state the constant term
Recognise additive patterns in First Nations Australians' material culture on Country/Place; represent using drawings, counters and numbers
Use matchsticks or connecting shapes to create a growing pattern; write the number sequence and describe the rule so someone else can replicate it with different materials
elaborations: creating a pattern sequence with materials, writing the associated number sequence, and describing it so someone else can replicate it; e.g. matchstick triangles 3, 5, 7 — 'Start with 3 and add 2 each time'
recognising patterns in the built environment: windows in carriages, wheels on cars
recognising the constant term and using it to identify missing elements
using dynamic geometric software or AI to create patterns that increase or decrease by a constant amount
recognising additive patterns on Country/Place and in First Nations Australians' material culture

AC9M2A02.minimum_width: Apply two different strategies (doubles, near doubles, counting on, combinations to 10, bridging to 10) to addition facts within 20.
AC9M2A02.typical_width: Recall addition facts to 20 with proficiency using all five strategy types; derive related subtraction facts using part-part-whole reasoning; demonstrate fluency (prompt response) across the full range of facts to 20.
wider: Limited width — addition fact recall is a fluency skill; the content does not vary meaningfully across contexts at Year 2. Extension involves applying recalled facts to two-digit addition or deriving related subtraction facts. Width investment means varied practice formats (oral, written, games, ten-frame visuals) rather than new phenomena.
Systematically record all partitions of 10 (and 20); explain patterns noticed; connect to addition and subtraction facts
AC9M2A02.width_notes: depth_fallback used: recall of addition facts is a fluency skill. Genuine enrichment is application of known facts (two-digit addition, related subtraction) rather than more contexts for the same facts.
elaborations: using ten-frames or connecting cubes to develop strategies: doubles, near doubles, counting on, combinations to 10, bridging to 10
partitioning and rearranging collections to practise facts to 20; using part-part-whole diagrams to develop subtraction facts
using partitioning to record facts systematically; e.g. all ways 10 birds can be spread among 2 trees

AC9M2A03.minimum_width: Double numbers within 20 using materials; state the related 'multiply by 2' fact; halve at least three even numbers within 20.
AC9M2A03.typical_width: Recall multiplication facts for twos with fluency; derive related division facts; connect doubling and halving as inverse operations; apply across doubling/halving games within 20.
wider: Limited width — twos multiplication fact recall is a fluency skill. Extension involves applying known twos facts to derive facts from other tables or to recognise even/odd patterns — these go further rather than broadening application of twos facts.
Investigate doubles and near-doubles: use double 5 = 10 to derive double 6 and double 4; extend across all numbers within 20
AC9M2A03.width_notes: depth_fallback used: recall of twos facts is a fluency skill. The elaborations are all variants of the same practise activity rather than distinct phenomena.
elaborations: recognising and relating terms: double, twice, multiply by 2, halve, divide by 2; using physical and virtual materials
doubling and halving collections to practise multiplication/division facts for twos
establishing doubles and near doubles: use double 5 = 10 to find double 6 and double 4
developing fluency with doubling and halving within 20; playing doubling and halving games

AC9M2M01.minimum_width: Measure one object using an informal unit for one attribute (length, capacity or mass); count the units; explain why the unit must be uniform.
AC9M2M01.typical_width: Measure and compare objects using appropriate uniform informal units for length, capacity and mass; justify unit choice; explain why smaller units give greater accuracy and produce larger counts for the same object.
wider: Compare the capacity of several containers using sand and different-sized units; explain the inverse relationship between unit size and count
Use balance scales to compare the mass of several objects using informal units; explain why units must be the same mass
Investigate First Nations Australians' use of body parts as uniform informal measurement units; discuss how a standard is maintained across different people
Investigate First Nations Australians' measurement of animal tracks (length, width, depth) to understand animal behaviour
elaborations: choosing suitable informal units to measure length; justifying choice of longer unit for long objects, shorter unit for more accuracy
comparing capacity of containers using sand and a spoon or cup; explaining why smaller units give more accuracy
using balance scales to compare mass; explaining why informal units must be the same mass
demonstrating why different shoe lengths give different measurements for the same distance
investigating First Nations Australians' use of body parts as uniform informal units
investigating measurable attributes used by First Nations Australians to understand animal behaviour: tracks

AC9M2M02.minimum_width: Identify and represent one-half and one-quarter of a shape; confirm both parts of the half are equal and all four parts of the quarter are equal.
AC9M2M02.typical_width: Identify common uses of halves, quarters and eighths; represent in shapes, objects and events including food, cooking measures, sport, time and position; explain that all parts must be equal.
wider: Investigate cup and spoon cooking measures: what half or quarter of a cup means; compare to the full measure using sand or water
Discuss halves and quarters in sporting events (AFL quarters/half time); connect to clock language (half past, quarter past)
Recognise halves and quarters describing lengths, positions and distances; e.g. halfway point in a race
elaborations: demonstrating how food items can be cut in halves, quarters or eighths by halving; ensuring parts are equal
investigating cup and spoon measures in cooking; comparing half/quarter measures to the full measure
demonstrating halves and quarters in folding activities
recognising halves and quarters describing lengths, positions and distances
discussing halves and quarters in sporting events; recognising half or quarter of an hour

AC9M2M03.minimum_width: Locate a specific date on a monthly calendar; count the days between two events in the same month.
AC9M2M03.typical_width: Locate specific dates; identify days of the week; determine the date 2 weeks before or after a given date; count days between events within and across months; create and use a class calendar.
wider: Model 'How many days left in this year?' by adding remaining days across months using a calendar
Locate and discuss culturally significant dates (ANZAC Day, Diwali, Ramadan, Easter); investigate why some dates change each year
Investigate the number of days in each month; discuss why months have different lengths
elaborations: using calendars to locate specific dates and identify the day; determining a date 2 weeks prior or after
creating a class calendar with specific relevant dates entered
using addition and a calendar to model how many days are left in this year
identifying and locating dates: school holidays, ANZAC Day, Easter, Diwali, Ramadan

AC9M2M04.minimum_width: Read an analog clock to the hour and half-hour; identify the hour and minute hand.
AC9M2M04.typical_width: Recognise and read the time to the hour, half-hour and quarter-hour; explain 'half past', 'quarter past' and 'quarter to'; connect hand positions to the time unit; create an analog clock from a paper plate.
wider: Divide a clockface into halves and quarters; connect the subdivisions to time-telling; connect quarter-past to a quarter-turn of the minute hand
Investigate the movement of both hands: how long does each take to go around? What does each rotation represent?
Compare analog and digital representations of the same time; discuss what information each format provides
elaborations: creating an analog clock from a paper plate; explaining hand movements and time units
recognising the relationship between hand movement and duration; connecting 'half past' to halfway around
dividing a clockface into halves and quarters; explaining 'quarter past' and 'quarter to'

AC9M2M05.minimum_width: Demonstrate a quarter turn and a half turn; use 'clockwise' and 'anticlockwise' correctly for at least one context.
AC9M2M05.typical_width: Identify, describe and demonstrate quarter, half, three-quarter and full turns in everyday situations; use clockwise and anticlockwise language; give and follow turn instructions to navigate spaces and grids.
wider: Investigate turning objects in the school environment (handles, dials); draw labelled diagrams showing direction and amount
Give and follow turn instructions in a choreographed dance or movement sequence
Investigate clock hands: relate quarter-turns to quarter-hours; connect rotation to time
elaborations: identifying turning objects in the school environment; drawing labelled diagrams
demonstrating and describing half, quarter and full turns in a choreographed dance
investigating clock hands and relating quarter, half and full hours to angles and clockwise/anticlockwise
giving or following directions using quarter, half, three-quarter and full turns for grids or robots

AC9M2SP01.minimum_width: Identify the number of sides and name one pair of parallel sides in a polygon; use 'straight' and 'curved' correctly.
AC9M2SP01.typical_width: Recognise, compare and classify shapes using number of sides and spatial terms (opposite, parallel, curved, straight); sort by multiple properties; recognise shapes in different orientations as the same shape.
wider: Investigate shapes of different sporting fields; label sidelines, parallel lines, curved boundaries using spatial terms
Use digital tools to create shapes then drag vertices to produce irregular versions; describe what changes and what stays the same
Sort quadrilaterals by sub-properties (parallel sides, equal sides); investigate which have both
elaborations: sorting shapes by features: number of sides, equal sides, pairs of opposite parallel sides
manipulating shapes and recognising different orientations don't change the shape
investigating shapes of different sporting fields; describing and labelling features using spatial terms
creating regular shapes with digital tools; dragging vertices to produce irregular shapes

AC9M2SP02.minimum_width: Locate a named position on a simple map of a familiar space; follow at least three movement instructions to reach a target on a grid.
AC9M2SP02.typical_width: Locate positions in 2D representations of familiar spaces; follow and give directions using positional and turn language on grids and maps; adjust instructions when they don't achieve the intended result.
wider: Move through a 2D maze using directional language including clockwise, anticlockwise and quarter turns
Program a robotic toy to follow a path on a floor mat; verify the result and adjust instructions
Create a grid pathway requiring a partner to use specific turn instructions; write and test them
elaborations: interpreting maps of familiar places and identifying positions of key features
understanding that maps are used to give and receive directions
using a classroom seating plan to locate a position and giving directions to classmates
following and creating movement instructions for a 4×4 grid; using a robotic toy to follow a path
moving through a 2D maze using clockwise, anticlockwise, quarter turn and similar language

AC9M2ST01.minimum_width: Pose one question about a categorical variable; collect data using one method; sort into at least three categories; display in a list or table.
AC9M2ST01.typical_width: Acquire categorical data through surveys, observation, experiment and digital tools; sort into relevant categories; display in lists and tables; use counting strategies to identify totals per category and most/least common.
wider: Use software or AI tools to construct a survey; collect class data; sort and interpret; consider whether questions need modifying
Investigate 'How much rubbish is really rubbish?' by categorising objects: throw away, recycle, reuse
Observe students arriving before deciding on transport categories; discuss how prior observation improves category design
Explore ways First Nations Australians observe, collect, sort and record data; discuss how purpose shapes collection method
elaborations: posing a question about favourite things; recording in a table; identifying most/least popular
investigating 'How much rubbish is really rubbish?' by gathering data in categories
using software or AI to construct a survey; sorting and interpreting responses
observing students arriving before deciding on data categories
exploring ways First Nations Australians observe, collect, sort and record data

AC9M2ST02.minimum_width: Create two different representations of the same small dataset; confirm both show the same totals per category.
AC9M2ST02.typical_width: Create different graphical representations (picture graphs, column graphs, tally charts, dot plots) of the same data using software where appropriate; compare two representations; identify common and distinctive features; describe ease of interpretation.
wider: Compare a picture graph with a column graph of the same data; say how they are the same and different
Create three representation types for the same data; rank from easiest to hardest to interpret and justify
Collect country-of-birth class data; create two different pictographs; compare and interpret
elaborations: creating 2 different graphical representations of the same data; comparing; e.g. picture graph vs column graph of favourite colour
creating lists, tally charts, column graphs and picture graphs; describing ease of interpretation
using digital tools including AI to create picture graphs with one-to-one correspondence
comparing picture graphs with column graphs of the same data; saying how they are same and different
using dot plots, sticker charts, picture graphs, bar charts and column graphs to represent data
